The word scab has a few distinct meanings depending on the context.
1. The Most Common Meaning: A Healing Crust on a Wound

When you get a cut, a scrape, or any open wound on your skin, your body immediately starts to heal itself. Blood flows out, and within minutes it begins to thicken and dry. Over the next day or so, this dried blood and dead tissue hardens into a rough, brownish-red crust that sits right on top of the wound. That crust is called a scab.

The scab is not just a side effect — it is nature's bandage. It protects the soft, healing skin underneath from dirt, bacteria, and further injury. Once the new skin has fully grown back beneath it, the scab dries out further and falls off on its own.

"He fell off his bicycle and scraped his knee badly, but by the next morning a scab had already formed."

"She kept picking at the scab, which is why the wound took so long to heal."

A key thing to know: picking or peeling a scab before it is ready can reopen the wound, cause bleeding, and even leave a permanent scar. This is why you will often hear the advice, "Don't pick the scab."

The word can also be used loosely to refer to a similar crusty formation on animal skin or plant surfaces when they are damaged or diseased — but in everyday conversation, it almost always refers to the one on human skin.
2. A Labor/Workplace Meaning: A Worker Who Crosses a Strike

This is a very different — and very loaded — meaning of the word.

When a group of workers feel they are being treated unfairly by their employer (for example, they are being paid too little, or their working conditions are unsafe), they may organize a strike. A strike means they collectively refuse to show up for work. The purpose is to pressure the employer: no workers means no production, which costs the employer money, which forces them to negotiate.

Now, here is where the word "scab" comes in. If someone — either an existing worker who refused to join the strike, or a new person hired from outside — crosses the picket line (the symbolic or literal line that the striking workers stand at) and goes in to do the work that the striking workers abandoned, that person is called a scab.

The striking workers see this as a betrayal and a threat, because a scab weakens the entire strike. If the employer can simply replace striking workers with scabs, the strike loses its power.

"When the factory workers went on strike, the company bused in scabs from another city to keep the production line running."

"Many of the original workers never forgave him for being a scab during the 1987 strike."

This is a strongly negative and insulting term. It is used by workers and labor unions to shame and condemn those who undermine a strike. You would not use this word in a neutral or positive way — it carries real anger and moral judgment. In formal writing or journalism, the same person might be called a strikebreaker or a replacement worker, but on the street or among workers, "scab" is the word that carries the full weight of contempt.

Occasionally — especially in British English and Australian English — "scab" is used as a general insult to call someone a mean, selfish, stingy, or despicable person. This usage is less common and quite informal.

"Don't be a scab — share your lunch with him."

This meaning grew naturally out of the labor meaning (where a scab is seen as a selfish, disloyal person) and from the wound meaning (where a scab is something ugly and undesirable). But this general insult usage is not very common in everyday conversation today, particularly outside of Britain and Australia.

In agriculture and botany, "scab" refers to a fungal or bacterial disease that causes rough, hardened, discolored patches on the surface of fruits, vegetables, or leaves. The patches look like — and are named after — the scabs on wounded skin. You will see this term used by farmers, gardeners, and plant scientists.

Common examples include apple scab (a fungal disease that creates dark, rough spots on apple skin) and potato scab (which creates rough, corky patches on the skin of potatoes).

"The apple harvest was poor this year because of scab."

"Rotating your crops can help prevent potato scab from spreading in the soil."

This meaning is specific to agricultural and botanical contexts. You would rarely encounter it in general daily conversation unless you work with plants or crops.

ContextWhat "scab" means

To summarize cleanly: the word "scab" in its noun form has one physical meaning and several human or figurative ones.

In its physical sense, it is the dry, hardened crust your body forms to protect a healing wound — something familiar to everyone. In its social and political sense, it is a harsh insult for a worker who betrays a strike, one of the strongest pieces of contempt in the vocabulary of organized labor. In a broader but less common informal sense, it is a general put-down for a selfish or unpleasant person. And in the specific world of agriculture, it names a type of plant disease characterized by rough, crusty patches.

The tone of the word ranges from neutral and clinical (when talking about a wound) to deeply offensive and charged (when used in the labor context). Always pay attention to context when you hear it, because the same word can mean something completely harmless or something intensely provocative depending on who is saying it and why.
